performers: Sviatoslav Richter; Warsaw National Philharmonic Orchestra; Stanisław Wisłocki
intro: Sviatoslav Richter and Stanisław Wisłocki perform the finale of the Piano Concerto No. 2, Op. 18, marked Allegro scherzando. Its broad melody is first played softly by oboe and violas, and after quick exchanges and a solo flourish it returns at the end in C major for the full orchestra.

sections.label: Intro · Strings, E major to C minor
sections.mNote: Short string figures move from E major to C minor.

sections.label: A · Piano leaps alternating with quick wind
sections.mNote: A short, sharply accented tune follows the solo flourish.

sections.label: B · Oboe and violas play in B♭
sections.mNote: Moderato; the piano rests for the long melody.

sections.label: Dev · First-theme figures, piano and orchestra
sections.mNote: Piano and orchestra trade the first theme’s figures.

sections.label: B′ · Flute and violins in D♭
sections.mNote: The long tune returns a minor third higher.

sections.label: Coda · Piano phrases accelerating to Presto
sections.mNote: Piano figures accelerate towards Presto and a solo flourish.

sections.label: B″ · Long theme in C major, Maestoso
sections.mNote: Maestoso; winds and strings play the theme over piano chords.

cues.title: Orchestral introduction
cues.text: The strings begin with short phrases that pass between violins and cellos. Clarinets, bassoons and tuba accompany them quietly, and the piano rests. The introduction modulates from the Adagio’s E major back towards C minor.
cues.evidence: Gutheil full score, Boosey & Hawkes reprint, pp. 68–69: quiet strings, clarinets, bassoons and tuba. The E major to C minor route is described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Concerto_No._2_(Rachmaninoff).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: First theme, piano
cues.text: The piano plays wide leaps across the keyboard, then short, accented figures. Flutes and clarinets reply, and the strings accompany pizzicato.
cues.evidence: Full score, pp. 70–72: solo leaps, accented piano theme, flute and clarinet replies and pizzicato strings. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/7/72/IMSLP528309-PMLP01953-Rachmaninoff_-_Piano_Concerto_No._2_(orch._score).pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Richter recording, Warsaw, 1959
cues.text: On 26 and 28 April 1959 Sviatoslav Richter recorded the concerto in the Philharmonic Hall, Warsaw, with Stanisław Wisłocki conducting the Warsaw orchestra. Deutsche Grammophon issued it on LP as DG 138 076, together with Rachmaninoff preludes.
cues.evidence: Pianist Discography lists the Richter–Wisłocki concerto as Deutsche Grammophon LP 138 076 (1959), recorded on 26 and 28 April 1959 in the Philharmonic Hall, Warsaw: https://pianistdiscography.com/discography/pianistLabel.php?cdnum=2186. The DG catalogue names Richter, the Warsaw Philharmonic Orchestra and Wisłocki for this concerto: https://www.deutschegrammophon.com/en/catalogue/products/rachmaninov-tchaikovsky-piano-concertos-richter-4901

cues.title: Second theme, oboe and violas
cues.text: Moderato. The oboe and violas introduce the long second theme in B♭ major. The piano rests while horns hold the harmony and cellos and basses play pizzicato underneath.
cues.evidence: Full score, p. 77: Moderato, B♭ major second theme for solo oboe and violas, horns and pizzicato lower strings.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Piano melody, rehearsal 31
cues.text: At rehearsal 31 the soloist returns with the long melody, marked mf dolce. The right hand plays it in chords above broken chords in the left hand. The orchestra is reduced to a few held notes in the wind and strings.
cues.evidence: Full score, Boosey & Hawkes reprint of the Gutheil edition, p. 78 (rehearsal 31): piano mf dolce, melody chords over left-hand arpeggios, a few sustained wind and string notes. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/7/72/IMSLP528309-PMLP01953-Rachmaninoff_-_Piano_Concerto_No._2_(orch._score).pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Visit to Tolstoy, early 1900
cues.text: In early 1900 Rachmaninoff and the bass Feodor Chaliapin performed one of his songs for Leo Tolstoy in the hope of encouragement. Tolstoy asked: “Tell me, do you really think anybody needs music like that?”
cues.evidence: Marc Mandel’s BSO note recounts the early-1900 meeting and quotes Tolstoy’s response to Rachmaninoff and Chaliapin. https://www.bso.org/works/piano-concerto-no-2-6

cues.title: Return of the first theme
cues.text: The short figures of the first theme return to the foreground. The piano plays chords high on the keyboard, and winds, brass and strings reply in short bursts. These phrases occupy most of the development.
cues.evidence: Full score, pp. 83–85: high piano chords and orchestral exchanges; the development’s reliance on the first theme is described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Concerto_No._2_(Rachmaninoff).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Treatment by Nikolai Dahl, 1900
cues.text: From January to April 1900 Rachmaninoff saw the psychiatrist Nikolai Dahl every day. Dahl used hypnosis, and each session repeated one phrase: “You will begin to write your concerto.” Rachmaninoff was composing again by the summer, and he dedicated the finished concerto to Dahl.
cues.evidence: Marc Mandel’s BSO note describes the daily sessions from January to April 1900, Dahl’s work with hypnosis, the repeated phrases and the dedication “to Mr. N. Dahl”: https://www.bso.org/works/piano-concerto-no-2-6

cues.title: Partial première, Moscow, 1900
cues.text: On 15 December 1900, at a benefit concert in Moscow, Rachmaninoff played the second and third movements with Siloti conducting. The audience received them with great success, and the first movement had not yet been written. The complete concerto was first performed on 9 November 1901, with the same soloist and conductor.
cues.evidence: Marc Mandel’s BSO note gives the 15 December 1900 performance of the second and third movements, the benefit concert, Siloti as conductor and the complete première on 9 November 1901: https://www.bso.org/works/piano-concerto-no-2-6

cues.title: Second theme in D♭ major
cues.text: The long melody returns in D♭ major, Moderato, played by flute and first violins. The piano rests again before taking it up. The theme is a minor third higher than at its first appearance.
cues.evidence: Full score, pp. 97–99: Moderato, D♭ major second theme for flute and first violins, then piano.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Piano takes the tune, rehearsal 37
cues.text: At a tempo (rehearsal 37) the piano takes the tune from the flute and violins, again marked mf dolce. Right-hand chords carry the melody above rolling left-hand arpeggios. The orchestra thins once more to a few held notes.
cues.evidence: Full score, p. 98 (rehearsal 37): a tempo, piano mf dolce, melody chords over left-hand arpeggios, with sustained clarinet and bassoon notes and arco low strings.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Popular song adaptation
cues.text: The long melody of the finale became the basis of the song Full Moon and Empty Arms. Frank Sinatra recorded it.
cues.evidence: Marc Mandel’s BSO note identifies the song’s source in the finale; Sinatra’s recording is documented in the concerto’s reception account. https://www.bso.org/works/piano-concerto-no-2-6 and https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Concerto_No._2_(Rachmaninoff)

cues.title: Piano entry with accelerando
cues.text: Short phrases pass between the woodwinds and strings. The piano enters p, with poco a poco accelerando marked above its repeated figures. The bass begins to move, and the tempo increases towards the final flourish.
cues.evidence: Full score, p. 103 and following: orchestral fragments, piano entrance at p and poco a poco accelerando.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Presto and piano flourish
cues.text: At the Presto the orchestra plays fff chords, then rests under long fermatas marked lunga. The piano plays a quasi glissando across the keyboard and continues to a fermata of its own. The Maestoso follows.
cues.evidence: Full score, p. 108: Presto, fff orchestral chords, lunga fermatas over rests and the piano’s quasi glissando; p. 109: piano figures ending on a fermata before Maestoso.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Maestoso in C major
cues.text: In the Maestoso the long melody returns in C major in the winds and strings, above full chords in the piano. Horns, trombones and tuba support it. The melody first heard on the oboe is now played by the full orchestra.
cues.evidence: Full score, pp. 109–112: C major Maestoso, expanded wind and string melody, piano chords and lower-brass support.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Più vivo and final cadence
cues.text: At Più vivo the piano resumes quick figures after the broad melody. Over repeated orchestral chords the music drives to the final C major cadence. The concerto ends with four emphatic attacks.
cues.evidence: Full score, pp. 112–116: Più vivo, quick piano figures and final C major cadence with four-attack closing rhythm.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The piano enters in C minor
transitions.from: Intro · Strings, E major to C minor
transitions.to: A · Piano leaps alternating with quick wind
transitions.how: The short string phrases build into an orchestral crescendo. The piano enters with a flourish and then moves between low bass notes and high figures in C minor. As its accented theme takes shape, flutes and clarinets reply over pizzicato strings.
transitions.evidence: Full score, pp. 68–72: introduction, solo flourish, first theme and pizzicato accompaniment.

transitions.title: Oboe and violas take the melody
transitions.from: A · Piano leaps alternating with quick wind
transitions.to: B · Oboe and violas play in B♭
transitions.how: A ritardando slows the piano’s broken chords. At Moderato the soloist rests, and oboe and violas begin the B♭ major melody. Horns hold quiet chords, and cellos and basses play the bass line pizzicato beneath the long phrase.
transitions.evidence: Full score, p. 77: ritardando, Moderato and the B♭ major oboe-and-viola theme.

transitions.title: Piano run and ff chords open development
transitions.from: B · Oboe and violas play in B♭
transitions.to: Dev · First-theme figures, piano and orchestra
transitions.how: The lyrical group closes in B♭ major and is followed by forceful exchanges. The piano climbs through a quick run and strikes high chords at ff. Winds, brass and strings reply with short, accented phrases. The development is built on the small figures of the first theme.
transitions.evidence: Full score, pp. 83–85; the first-theme basis of the development is described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Concerto_No._2_(Rachmaninoff).

transitions.title: Long theme returns in D♭ major
transitions.from: Dev · First-theme figures, piano and orchestra
transitions.to: B′ · Flute and violins in D♭
transitions.how: The piano slows through Meno mosso and a ritardando, then stops at Moderato. Flute and first violins play the long theme again in D♭ major. Clarinets and bassoons hold the harmony, and the lower strings pluck the bass notes.
transitions.evidence: Full score, p. 97: Meno mosso, ritardando and D♭ major Moderato with flute and violin melody.

transitions.title: Short phrases accelerate towards Presto
transitions.from: B′ · Flute and violins in D♭
transitions.to: Coda · Piano phrases accelerating to Presto
transitions.how: The long melody breaks into short phrases in the wind and strings. The piano enters at a quiet dynamic over a held low C. Its repeated figures are marked poco a poco accelerando. The horns join the rhythm. When the bass begins to move, the passage accelerates to Presto.
transitions.evidence: Full score, pp. 103–108: orchestral fragments, quiet piano entrance over C, accelerando and Presto.

transitions.title: Solo flourish leads into C major Maestoso
transitions.from: Coda · Piano phrases accelerating to Presto
transitions.to: B″ · Long theme in C major, Maestoso
transitions.how: The orchestra plays a short Presto passage. A long fermata over rests follows, and the piano then plays alone. Its flourish crosses the keyboard and slows into the Maestoso. The second melody returns in C major in the winds and strings, above full chords in the piano and a low C in the bass.
transitions.evidence: Full score, pp. 108–110: Presto, long orchestral rest, solo flourish and C major Maestoso.

source.title: Rachmaninoff, Piano Concerto No. 2, full score, Gutheil engraving in Boosey & Hawkes reprint, plate B. & H. 16674
source.locator: Printed pp. 68–116: orchestral introduction, quick piano theme, B♭ major oboe-and-viola melody, D♭ major return and C major Maestoso.

timeline.note: Quiet string phrases pass between violins and cellos, supported by clarinet, bassoon and tuba (pp. 68–69).
The orchestra plays a crescendo and the piano enters with a run across the keyboard (pp. 69–70).
The piano plays a short, accented tune, and flute and clarinet answer it over plucked strings (pp. 71–72).
The piano exchanges quick phrases with woodwinds, horns and strings (pp. 73–75).
Oboe and violas play the B♭ major theme at Moderato; horns hold chords and lower strings play the bass pizzicato (p. 77).
The piano plays the long melody above its own broken chords, with quiet woodwinds and strings (pp. 78–79).
The piano plays high chords, and winds, brass and strings play short bursts between them (pp. 83–85).
Wind and brass phrases enter around the piano’s running notes and chords (pp. 91–93).
Flute and first violins bring back the long tune in D♭ major; clarinets and bassoons hold the harmony (p. 97).
The piano takes up the D♭ major melody over sustained woodwind and string notes (pp. 98–99).
The full orchestra plays through the Presto, and after a long pause the piano is left alone (p. 108).
The piano’s solo flourish crosses the keyboard between Presto and Maestoso (pp. 108–109).
Winds and strings play the C major Maestoso above piano chords, horns and lower brass; trumpets and cymbals rest (pp. 109–110).
At Più vivo, quick piano figures lead to full-orchestra chords with timpani, bass drum and cymbals (pp. 112–116).

composer.epithet: Russian composer and pianist who earned his living at the piano in exile and whose music uses the sound of the bells of his childhood.
facts: Zverev and Siloti at the piano; Taneyev and Arensky in composition

quote.text: I feel like a ghost wandering in a world grown alien. I cannot cast out the old way of writing, and I cannot acquire the new.
quote.source: Rachmaninoff to Leonard Liebling, 1939; published in The Musical Courier, 5 April 1943

composer.background:
“My hearty thanks to the old man for not having forgotten about me!” Rachmaninoff wrote to the singer Mikhail Slonov on 26 December 1892. The old man was Tchaikovsky, who had praised his opera Aleko in a newspaper interview. Rachmaninoff was nineteen and had recently graduated from the Moscow Conservatory with its Great Gold Medal. Tchaikovsky helped get the opera into the Bolshoi, and in May 1893 he sat in the audience and applauded.

His childhood had been less settled. He was born into a landowning family and grew up at Oneg, near Novgorod, until his father’s financial failures forced a move to St Petersburg. He entered the Conservatory there in 1883. His parents separated, his sister Sofia died of diphtheria, and his schoolwork went badly. His grandmother took him to Orthodox services, where he heard the choirs and bells he remembered all his life. In 1885 his cousin Alexander Siloti recommended that he move to Moscow to study with the piano teacher Nikolai Zverev, who was known for his strictness.
